DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU

stack. The panels show the unoptimized configuration and the simulated results after 10, 50, and 78 iterations.
Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable en-
forcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast
simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based
on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or posi-
tional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration
through geometric barriers and continuous collision detection (CCD). How-
ever, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space
finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid compo-
nents retain many vertex degrees of freedom (DoFs). We present DiffGIPC,
a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interact-
ing deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable
rest-shape design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while
retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients ac-
count for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other
objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in
one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-
system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse
problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost
of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects
supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses
across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Ex-
periments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0×

1    Introduction
Gradient-based design, system identification, and control often op-
timize one object’s parameters for their effect on another object. A
hanger’s shape determines whether a garment remains supported.
An initial velocity determines where another body moves after
collision, and a robot command changes the motion of a grasped
deformable object. In each case, the gradient must follow forces
transmitted through contact and the subsequent motion. Comput-
ing these derivatives efficiently is particularly challenging when a
scene combines deformable objects with detailed, nearly rigid com-
ponents: the representation must resolve the interactions without
making every stiff component expensive to differentiate.
Existing methods address different parts of this problem. Differ-
entiable projective-dynamics methods, including DiffPD and Dif-
fCloth [Du et al.2021; Li et al.2022], accelerate repeated solves
through local-global iterations and matrix prefactorization. Repre-
senting nearly rigid components as stiff deformable meshes nev-
ertheless retains vertex-level motion DoFs, increasing simulation

and differentiation costs even when only near-rigid motion is re-
quired [Lai et al.2026]. ADD [Geilinger et al.2020] provides fully
implicit, two-way coupled rigid and deformable dynamics with ana-
lytic adjoints, but uses penalty-based normal contact, which does not
strictly prevent interpenetration. DiffIPC [Huang et al.2024c] differ-
entiates fully implicit FEM dynamics with friction, using IPC barriers
and continuous collision detection to maintain non-penetration. Its
full-space representation, however, carries the motion DoFs of every
stiff component into the backward solve, making repeated evalua-
tions costly in its CPU implementation. The resulting opportunity
is to combine contact-coupled differentiation with compact motion
coordinates and efficient GPU execution.
We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated framework for differ-
entiating coupled FEM-affine IPC simulations (Figure 2). Building
on the forward formulation of StiffGIPC [Huang et al.2025a], we
derive frame-wise adjoints directly in the mixed motion coordinates.
Full-space FEM retains the freedom needed for local deformation,
while each affine body contributes only twelve motion DoFs regard-
less of its surface resolution. Contact and joint derivatives couple
interacting bodies within each frame. Inertia and friction make the
time integration equations depend on earlier states. The backward
systems therefore remain compact while preserving cross-object
coupling and the temporal dependencies required for coupled in-
verse problems.
Compact motion coordinates alone do not provide shape or con-
trol gradients. Changing an affine rest surface changes its mass, the
positions at which contact is evaluated, and the maps that convert
point-space forces to affine coordinates. Under friction, the same rest
change also moves the previous-frame points used to define sliding
and the lagged contact quantities. We differentiate these dependen-
cies explicitly, together with initial states and revolute or prismatic
joint controls, and accumulate them in parallel without enlarging
the adjoint system. To retain the advantage of compact systems,
conditional CUDA Graphs are employed to keep preconditioned
conjugate gradient (PCG) iterations and convergence checks on the
GPU, thereby reducing the overhead of repeated kernel launches
and CPU–GPU synchronization. A PyTorch interface connects these
physical gradients to user-defined parameter maps and losses.
In summary, our contributions are:
•Coupled FEM-affine adjoints for differentiable IPC. We
derive trajectory adjoints in mixed FEM and affine coordi-
nates, preserving contact, friction, and joint coupling while
using only twelve motion DoFs per affine body.
•Affine-body derivatives for shape design and articu-
lated control. We derive gradients for affine rest shapes,
initial states, and joint controls, including shape-dependent
inertia and frictional contact.
•A reusable GPU optimization pipeline. We develop a
GPU-parallel adjoint and gradient-accumulation pipeline
with conditional CUDA Graphs and a PyTorch interface for
design, system identification, and control.
•Fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC. We present the
first fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC framework for cou-
pled nearly rigid and deformable bodies, with substantial
speedups demonstrated across contact-rich inverse prob-
lems.
Our evaluation examines the benefits of GPU execution and com-
pact motion representations across contact-rich inverse problems.
For comparison with DiffIPC, we retain full-space FEM in both
systems and use relatively low-resolution benchmarks to keep eval-
uation times manageable for the CPU-based baseline. Even at these
resolutions, DiffGIPC achieves 12.3–34.1×speedups in complete
backward evaluation and 10.6–60.9×speedups in combined forward
and backward evaluation, covering initial motion, rest shape, mate-
rial, and friction optimization. A separate resolution study examines
how performance scales with geometric detail and the additional

DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU•    3
benefit of affine coordinates. Further experiments demonstrate cloth
design, affine shape optimization, stable placement, and articulated
control. The source code of our framework will be released.
2    Related Work
Efficient differentiable simulation and contact.  Inverse problems
such as parameter identification from measured motion [Hahn et al.
2019; Jatavallabhula et al.2021] require repeated simulation and
gradient evaluations, making the efficiency of both computations
important. Diff Taichi automates the differentiation of parallel sim-
ulation programs through source-code transformations [Hu et al.
2020]. Brax integrates differentiable rigid-body simulation and learn-
ing on accelerators, reducing data transfer between simulation and
optimization [Freeman et al.2021]. ChainQueen [Hu et al.2019] uses
explicit MLS-MPM with parallel local updates, but stiff materials
require small time steps. Implicit deformable simulation methods [Li
et al.2026; Liang et al.2019; Rojas et al.2021] offer greater time-step
stability, at the cost of solving linear systems during both simula-
tion and differentiation. Projective dynamics (PD) reduces this cost
through local projections and a global system whose matrix can be
prefactorized for fixed discretization and coefficients [Bouaziz et al.
2014]. DiffPD reuses this factorization in its backward iterations [Du
et al.2021]. Quasi-Newton methods support more general hyper-
elastic energies through efficient approximate systems [Liu et al.
2017], and DiffQN further reduces differentiation costs by reusing
factorizations from the forward simulation [Cai et al.2025]. More
recently, DiffPhD combines GPU factor reuse with techniques for
heterogeneous and hyperelastic materials [Lai et al. 2026].
For contact-rich inverse problems, these computational benefits
must also be considered alongside the contact response being differ-
entiated. DiffPD’s penalty formulation supports frictional sliding but
permits interpenetration, whereas its complementarity formulation
enforces non-penetration under a sticky-contact assumption [Du
et al.2021]. DiffCloth differentiates the dry-friction PD formulation
of Ly et al.[2020], supporting sliding cloth contact [Li et al.2022].
However, its self-collision treatment considers only vertex-vertex
pairs and does not handle vertex-face or edge-edge self-collisions.
DiffPhD supports Signorini-Coulomb contact on the GPU, but its
velocity-level enforcement can produce position drift under quasi-
static support [Lai et al.2026]. These limitations are particularly
relevant when the optimized behavior depends on sustained sup-
port, sliding, or contact between thin surfaces. They motivate ef-
ficient differentiation of contact models that preserve geometric
non-penetration throughout the simulated motion.
Differentiable contact and coupled dynamics.  Qiao et al.[2020] en-
able differentiable two-way coupling between rigid bodies and cloth,
using local impact zones to reduce the cost of collision handling
and differentiation. ADD provides fully implicit rigid-deformable
coupling with analytic adjoints [Geilinger et al.2020]. Its normal
penalty makes contact differentiable while allowing finite overlap.
Increasing the penalty stiffness reduces overlap at the cost of poorer
conditioning. IPC instead combines a geometric barrier with con-
tinuous collision detection to maintain intersection-free motion
from feasible initial configurations [Li et al.2020]. DiffIPC brings
this contact model to differentiable FEM simulation and supports
shape, material, friction, and initial-state optimization [Huang et al.
2024c]. It therefore provides a strong basis for inverse problems in
which penetration would change the intended interaction. However,
representing nearly rigid components with highly stiff, full-space
FEM retains vertex-level motion DoFs even when their local defor-
mation is negligible. In its CPU-based implementation, repeated
simulation and differentiation of these large systems remain costly.
DiffGIPC addresses this cost with coupled FEM-ABD adjoints and
GPU backward computation while retaining IPC’s geometric contact
safeguards.
Compact coordinates for coupled design and control.  Reducing mo-
tion DoFs addresses a cost that faster linear algebra alone does not
remove. Modal and adaptive subspaces reduce deformable motion
to a smaller set of directions [Barbič and James 2005; Trusty et al.
2024]. Their accuracy depends on whether those directions capture
the deformation induced by loads and contact. Hyper-reduced PD
also approximates local constraint projections [Brandt et al.2018],
while subspace mixed FEM combines reduced positions with stretch
variables to handle heterogeneous materials [Trusty et al.2023].
These approaches retain selected deformation modes and reduce
their evaluation cost. For components whose internal deformation
is negligible, rigid-body coordinates avoid resolving these modes al-
together. Rigid IPC preserves non-penetration in this representation
by accounting for curved rotational trajectories in collision detec-
tion [Ferguson et al.2021]. ABD relaxes exact rigidity through a stiff
orthogonality energy and uses twelve affine DoFs per body [Lan
et al.2022]. Its surface positions are linear in these DoFs, allowing
piecewise-linear collision trajectories and a pose-independent mass
matrix at fixed rest geometry. This offers a compact representation
for stiff parts, while full-space FEM retains local deformation where
it is needed. DiffGIPC carries both representations into the same
backward system, retaining contact, friction, and joint coupling
between bodies.
Compact rigid-body states have supported differentiable learning
and control [Belbute-Peres et al.2018; Degrave et al.2019], includ-
ing articulated dynamics in Nimble [Werling et al.2021]. Shape
optimization requires an additional distinction between the motion
representation and the geometry being designed. Contact-based as-
semblies and shock-protecting microstructures [Huang et al.2024b;
Tozoni et al.2021] use geometric changes to alter load transfer and
contact-dependent mechanical response. Pneumatic actuator design
and garment reconstruction [Gjoka et al.2024; Li et al.2025] likewise
optimize rest geometry through its effect on deformation. These
applications motivate retaining a rich design space even when the
motion state can be compact.
SDRS uses convex polyhedra and auxiliary separating planes to
maintain differentiability under large shape changes [Ye et al.2025].
Our focus is mesh-based design and control of affine bodies interact-
ing with deformable objects under IPC. Affine rest-shape changes
affect both the mass matrix and the maps from affine DoFs to surface
points. Differentiating these dependencies allows a body’s shape to
be optimized for its frictional interactions with other objects. Deriva-
tives of joint targets and forces likewise account for the coupled
response of articulated and deformable bodies. For a fixed motion
representation, additional design parameters do not enlarge the

4•    Huang et al.
per-frame backward system. Each affine body therefore contributes
only twelve motion DoFs, even when its rest shape is described
by many design parameters. Contact processing still depends on
surface resolution, while parameter-gradient evaluation requires
additional work as the number of design parameters grows.
GPU computation for trajectory adjoints.  Compact coordinates
reduce adjoint system size, while efficient linear solvers further
reduce the cost of trajectory differentiation. PD-based local-global
methods exploit a fixed global matrix to reuse precomputed factors.
Zeng et al.[2025] use a sparse representation of its inverse to ac-
celerate GPU forward simulation. DiffPhD adopts this strategy for
differentiable simulation, reusing an inverse factor across forward,
backward, and frictional-contact computations [Lai et al.2026]. In
IPC, however, the frame Hessian varies with deformation and con-
tact, so a fixed factorization cannot be reused across all adjoint
systems along a trajectory. Preconditioned iterative solvers provide
an alternative, with effective preconditioning reducing the number
of iterations [Chen et al.2021; Wu et al.2022]. GIPC parallelizes
IPC computation [Huang et al.2024a], while StiffGIPC provides
efficient FEM-ABD coupling and GPU solvers across a wide range
of stiffnesses [Huang et al.2025a], and AGIPC further reduces GPU
linear-solve costs through adaptive in-solve algebraic coarsening
[Wang et al.2026]. These methods advance GPU IPC efficiency,
with StiffGIPC supplying the forward simulation foundation for our
work.
DiffGIPC combines coupled frame-wise adjoint solves with paral-
lel gradient accumulation on the GPU. Compact affine coordinates
reduce PCG’s numerical workload, making repeated CPU kernel
launches and convergence synchronization more prominent. Con-
ditional CUDA Graphs reduce this overhead by keeping iteration
control and convergence checks on the GPU, with compatible graphs
reused across frames as the Hessian changes. After each solve, local
derivative products are accumulated in parallel to compute physical-
parameter gradients and update earlier-frame adjoint right-hand
sides.
3    A Unified Differentiable IPC Framework
The framework separates the coordinates needed to describe contact
geometry from those needed to solve motion. Collision and friction
derivatives are evaluated at world-space surface points and mapped
into a coupled system of FEM vertex positions and affine body
coordinates. This preserves cross-object derivatives while assigning
twelve motion DoFs to each affine body.
The forward formulation builds on StiffGIPC [Huang et al.2025a].
Simulation DoFs describe solved motion, whereas physical parame-
ters are inputs changed by the optimizer. One frame is an accepted
time step of lengthℎ, and mesh connectivity is fixed within each
differentiated trajectory. The state and incremental potential below
define the single-step adjoint. Section 4 extends it through time, Sec-
tion 5 supplies affine design and control derivatives, and Section 6
develops their GPU computation and task interface.

4    Frame-Wise Adjoint
The single-step adjoint captures interactions at one frame. A trajec-
tory also depends on how earlier motion changes later inertia and
friction. We account for these dependencies by backward substitu-
tion through the causal sequence of frame equations. Each reverse
frame solves one coupled FEM-affine system, then contributes to
the parameters and earlier states that influenced it. Algorithm 1
summarizes this recurrence. We derive its temporal structure and
then specify the inertia and friction terms, using the converged
states and recorded data that define the forward equations.
